topic: Discrete Convolutions: The Art of Mixing Signals
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Engineering

outline.topic: Discrete Convolutions: The Art of Mixing Signals
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Computer Science or Engineering

sections.title: The Big Idea: What is Convolution?
sections.content: Introduction to convolution as a mathematical 'mixer'. Explain that it combines two functions to show how the shape of one is modified by the other. Establish the 'Sliding Window' intuition.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Cleaning Robot' (the kernel) moving across a dusty floor (the input signal). The robot's brush shape determines how much dust is picked up at each specific spot as it passes over.

sections.title: Prerequisites: Signals and Kernels
sections.content: Define a discrete signal as a sequence of numbers (like coordinates on a grid). Introduce the 'Kernel' (or filter) as a small array of weights that defines the transformation rule. Explain index notation (n, k).
sections.example: An audio signal represented as a sequence of volume levels: [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]. A 'Smoothing Kernel' represented as: [0.5, 0.5].

sections.title: The Four-Step Algorithm: Flip, Shift, Multiply, Sum
sections.content: Break down the formula (f * g)[n] = Σ f[k]g[n-k]. 1. Flip the kernel. 2. Shift it to position 'n'. 3. Multiply overlapping elements. 4. Sum the results to get the output for that position.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Chef' (the formula) flipping a pancake-shaped filter, sliding it over a row of ingredients, multiplying the flavors, and serving the sum as a single bite.

sections.title: Graphical Visualization (The Sliding Animation)
sections.content: A frame-by-frame animation showing a stationary blue bar chart (Input) and a sliding, inverted red bar chart (Kernel). As they overlap, highlight the multiplication of heights and the resulting new yellow bar (Output) growing below.
sections.example: A 'Pulse Signal' [0, 1, 1, 1, 0] being convolved with a 'Triangle Kernel' to produce a smooth 'Mound' shape, demonstrating how convolution softens sharp edges.

sections.title: Application: Digital Image Filtering
sections.content: Extend the concept to 2D. Explain how a 3x3 matrix (kernel) slides over pixels in an image to perform operations like blurring, sharpening, or edge detection.
sections.example: A 'Robot Eye' (AI Camera) using a 'Sobel Kernel' to detect the edges of a cat in a photo. The convolution process highlights only the outlines, helping the robot identify the animal's shape.

sections.title: Summary and Takeaway
sections.content: Recap the importance of convolution in modern technology, specifically its role as the backbone of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and digital signal processing.
sections.example: The 'Hidden Hero' metaphor: Convolution is the silent engine behind Instagram filters and self-driving car vision.

storyboard.title: The Big Idea: What is Convolution?
lecture_lines: Convolution mixes two signals to create a new one.
One function's shape modifies the other's properties.
Imagine a sliding window transforming data as it moves.
animations: Create a grid of grey points #808080 representing 'Dusty Floor'.
Fade in a blue square #0000FF labeled 'Cleaning Robot (Kernel)'.
Animate the blue square sliding across the grey grid.
Change passed grey points to white #FFFFFF ('Clean Floor').
Display text 'Convolution = Input Signal ⊗ Filter Kernel' in gold #FFD700.

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: Signals and Kernels
lecture_lines: Discrete signals are simple sequences of numeric values.
Kernels are small weight arrays that define transformations.
Indices n and k track positions within these sequences.
animations: Draw a sequence of blue bars #0000FF labeled 'Signal f[n]'.
Draw a small red bar pair #FF0000 labeled 'Kernel g[k]'.
Highlight index 'n' on signal and 'k' on kernel with #00FF00.

storyboard.title: The Four-Step Algorithm: Flip, Shift, Multiply, Sum
lecture_lines: First, flip the kernel to reverse its order.
Second, shift the flipped kernel to your target index.
Third, multiply overlapping values from the signal and kernel.
Finally, sum these products for a single output point.
animations: Display red bars #FF0000; rotate 180 degrees to show 'Flip'.
Slide flipped bars horizontally to show 'Shift' to position n.
Pulse overlapping areas between Signal and Kernel in green #00FF00.
Show multiplication results as floating numbers above the overlap.
Create a yellow bar #FFFF00 representing the 'Sum' at position n.

storyboard.title: Graphical Visualization (The Sliding Animation)
lecture_lines: A stationary blue signal meets a sliding red kernel.
Observe how the overlapping regions generate new values.
Each step creates a point for the yellow output.
Notice how convolution smooths out sharp signal edges.
animations: Place a stationary blue pulse signal #0000FF on a timeline.
Animate a red triangle kernel #FF0000 sliding from left to right.
Draw a yellow curve #FFFF00 dynamically as the kernel slides.
Show the yellow curve smoothing the sharp edges of the pulse.
Highlight the 'Area under the Product' during the slide with #00FF00.

storyboard.title: Application: Digital Image Filtering
lecture_lines: Image convolution uses a two-dimensional sliding matrix.
These filters can blur, sharpen, or detect sharp edges.
Convolution enables computers to "see" outlines in images.
animations: Show a 6x6 pixel grid; move a 3x3 blue box #0000FF over it.
In a second grid, draw bright white edges #FFFFFF during movement.
Flash the text 'Edge Detection' in green #00FF00.

storyboard.title: Summary and Takeaway
lecture_lines: Convolution is the foundation of digital signal processing.
It powers modern AI vision and everyday photo filters.
This mathematical mixer transforms how we process information.
animations: Display 'CNN' and 'DSP' in bold cyan #00FFFF.
Show a flow of data points entering a 'Convolution' block.
Fade in labels: 'Self-Driving Cars', 'Photo Filters', 'AI'.
